kurz: A complete valuation walk-through from the first line of the income statement to the limit price in the order screen, with an assumptions log, three scenarios and stopping criteria.

bloecke.md:
A valuation model produces a single number. A decision, by contrast, needs a range, a written rationale and a threshold at which you act.

The company valued here is a fictitious German supplier of industrial sensor technology listed in the SDAX; all figures are an illustrative calculation. The figures for the 2025 financial year are as follows: revenue €640 million, reported EBIT €86.4 million, depreciation and amortisation €40.5 million (of which €6.5 million from a purchase price allocation), net financial debt €180 million including lease liabilities under IFRS 16, net pension obligation €35 million, goodwill €195 million, equity €340 million with a balance sheet total of €820 million. There are 20.0 million shares outstanding, or 20.6 million on a diluted basis. The share price is €32.00.

bloecke.titel: The nine stages of the walk-through
bloecke.unter: The order is fixed because the calculation easily aligns itself with the share price if you look at the price before the assumptions.

bloecke.md:
## Normalising the figures (stage 1)

There are three competing figures for EBIT. The income statement shows €86.4 million. The investor presentation shows an adjusted EBIT of €104.0 million, adjusted for €9.0 million of restructuring, €6.5 million of amortisation on the purchase price allocation and €2.1 million of share-based payment. You have to derive the third figure yourself, and it lies between the other two.

bloecke.titel: From reported to normalised EBIT (€m, illustrative calculation)
zeilen: incurred in four of the last five years
requires no reinvestment; the purchase price is already included in invested capital
causes real dilution; also appears in the denominator via the 20.6 million shares

bloecke.md: Adjusted figures are alternative performance measures. Since July 2016, the ESMA guidelines have required a definition for them, a reconciliation to the IFRS figure and consistent application over time. Two checks show whether an adjustment is appropriate. If the same item is adjusted every year, it is a recurring expense and not a one-off item. If only expenses are adjusted and never income, the adjustment shifts the result in one direction only. For financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2027, IFRS 18 requires disclosures on such management-defined measures.

Normalised EBIT is €92.9 million. The combined income tax rate is 31% and is made up of 15% corporation tax (Section 23(1) KStG, Corporation Tax Act) plus a 5.5% solidarity surcharge, together with trade tax (Gewerbesteuer), which results from the tax base rate (Messzahl) of 3.5% (Section 11(2) GewStG, Trade Tax Act) at a municipal multiplier (Hebesatz) of 435%. This produces a NOPAT of €64.1 million. Relative to invested capital of €520 million (equity of 340 plus financial debt of 180), this gives a ROIC of 12.3%. This is the most important metric in the whole walk-through, because it later limits how much growth can be worth.

## Assumptions log (stage 2)

The assumptions are written down before any calculation is done. The log is not a formality, because it is the only protection against deliberately changing, on the third attempt, the very assumption that delivers the desired result. Each line contains a value, its source and an honest assessment of how certain it is. Where an assumption noticeably changes the value, the counter-calculation is added.

zeilen: own normalisation from income statement and notes
forecast report under Section 289 HGB (Commercial Code), capped at the industry average
corporation tax, solidarity surcharge, trade tax at a 435% multiplier
yield on 10-year German federal bonds, 18 Sep 2026
two-year weekly beta against a European index
target capital structure of 80/20 instead of market values, to avoid circularity
below inflation target plus real growth

bloecke.md:
Two lines need an explanation. The first concerns the cost of capital. A cost of equity of 3.5 + 1.15 × 5.5 = 9.8% and a WACC of 8.5% look arbitrary. Yet they are almost exactly in line with the values that the KPMG cost of capital study 2025 found for mainly German companies (9.7% cost of equity, 8.5% WACC). That study, however, assumed a risk-free rate of 2.5%, whereas German federal bonds yield around 3.5% in September 2026. The risk premium and the base rate have to match; otherwise the total required return shifts without anyone noticing. For formal valuations under IDW S1, the base rate derived from the Bundesbank's Svensson yield curve applies in any case, not the yield on the day.

The second line is the steady-state ROIC. It links growth to capital requirements and thus prevents the most common error in the terminal value, namely perpetual growth that costs nothing.

bloecke.formel: g = ROIC × Reinvestment rate   →   Reinvestment rate = g / ROIC
bloecke.erklaerung: If a company is to grow in the steady state, it must keep part of its NOPAT in the business. The return on capital determines how large this part is.
variablen: return on capital in the steady state
share of NOPAT that cannot be distributed
bloecke.beispiel: With g = 1.75% and ROIC = 12.0%, the reinvestment rate is 14.6%. FCFF in year 6 = 79.3 × (1 − 0.146) = €67.7 million. Terminal value = 67.7 / (0.085 − 0.0175) = €1,003 million.

bloecke.md:
## Three scenarios (stage 3)

A point estimate is a statement about the future; three scenarios are a statement about the range. A range can be debated on its merits, and that is the purpose of the exercise. All three scenarios are calculated in the same way, with five explicit forecast years, free cash flow to the firm and a terminal value based on the reinvestment rate. This is followed by the bridge, that is, minus €180 million of net financial debt and €35 million of pensions, divided by 20.6 million diluted shares.

bloecke.titel: The three scenarios (illustrative calculation, amounts in €m)

bloecke.md:
The scenario-weighted expected value is 0.30 × 18.34 + 0.50 × 31.48 + 0.20 × 48.47 = €30.94. The good case is 2.6 times the bad one. This range is wide, but it reflects the uncertainty honestly. In the base case, 77% of the enterprise value comes from the terminal value and therefore from two numbers that nobody can observe.

The question of which single assumption moves the value most is more revealing than the weighting. To answer it, only one input is changed at a time, and all the others stay at the base-case setting.

bloecke.titel: Value per share when one assumption changes at a time (illustrative calculation, euros)
bloecke.unter: Half a percentage point on the WACC changes the value more than one and a half percentage points of revenue growth; the most uncertain assumption therefore has the greatest effect.

bloecke.md: If revenue growth falls from 4.0% to 2.5%, this costs only €2.25 per share, whereas half a percentage point more WACC costs €3.04. With a ROIC of 12% and a cost of capital of 8.5%, each additional euro invested earns only 3.5 percentage points of excess return. It also has to be financed first, in the model through capital expenditure of 7.5% of revenue against depreciation of 5.3% and through 22% working capital on every increase in revenue. The WACC, by contrast, affects all explicit forecast years and the terminal value at the same time, where it sits in the denominator alongside g.

## Cross-check (stage 4)

At the current share price, the enterprise value is €640 million of market capitalisation plus €180 million of net financial debt plus €35 million of pensions, €855 million in total. Relative to normalised EBIT, this corresponds to a multiple of 9.2; relative to reported EBIT, 9.9; and relative to the company's adjusted figure, 8.2. The same company therefore has three different multiples. Four European competitors of comparable size trade at a median of 12.4 times. That would give €45.48 per share, around 40% above the share price.

zeilen: that the peer companies have the same capital intensity
around 4.3% revenue growth with unchanged margin

bloecke.md:
When two methods contradict each other, the one whose assumptions can be written down is the one that counts, even if the other delivers a more pleasing result. The multiple is the outlier here, and the reason for this can be explained. EV/EBIT is an earnings metric. It does not take into account that this company invests 7.5% of revenue while only 5.3% is depreciated. Less cash is therefore left over from EBIT than at a peer company with lower reinvestment requirements. A peer multiple contains the peers' assumptions without disclosing them.

The reverse DCF takes the share price as given and solves for growth. With all other assumptions unchanged, a price of €32.00 corresponds to around 4.3% revenue growth over five years. This expectation is not far-fetched and roughly matches your own. The market and your own calculation therefore agree. Buying at the current price, however, then means paying full value.

bloecke.formel: Margin of safety = (Value per share − Price) / Value per share
bloecke.erklaerung: The margin of safety is a buffer against errors in your own valuation. It does not indicate the expected return.
bloecke.beispiel: In the base case, the margin of safety is (31.48 − 32.00) / 31.48 = −1.7%. The buying threshold at a 30% margin of safety is 31.48 × 0.70 = €22.04.

bloecke.titel: Margin of safety relative to the base value
bloecke.unter: With a range of €18 to €48, a margin of safety below 30% is not enough of a buffer.

bloecke.md:
## Decision (stage 5)

The decision is not to buy, to put the share on the watchlist and to plan a limit price of €22.00. Three points about this are easily overlooked.

First, dilution flips the sign of the margin of safety. Divided by 20.0 million shares outstanding, the base value is €32.43, which is above the share price. Divided by 20.6 million diluted shares, it is €31.48, which is below the share price. This has no consequences for the decision, because both values are well above the €22 threshold. The threshold is there to absorb differences like these.

Second, the margin of safety does not protect completely. If you bought at €22, the pessimistic case at €18.34 would still be 17% lower. A 30% margin makes the bad case bearable, but not harmless. Investing despite a range spanning a factor of 2.6 therefore calls for a limited position size. This follows from the range itself and is not a recommendation.

Third, the value is before personal tax. Realised capital gains and dividends are subject to 25% flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) under Section 32d(1) EStG (Income Tax Act) plus a 5.5% solidarity surcharge on it under Section 4 SolzG 1995 (Solidarity Surcharge Act), 26.375% in total, after deducting the saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000 for single persons (Section 20(9) EStG). Just under three quarters of a realised undervaluation is left over.

Not every deviation is a reason to adjust the model. Four findings end the calculation instead of correcting it.

1. The data basis is not reliable. Signs of this are receivables growing much faster than revenue, operating cash flow below net profit for several years, a change of auditor or chief financial officer, or a qualified audit opinion. Wirecard had unqualified audit opinions for years, and €1.9 billion of trust account balances (around a quarter of the balance sheet total) did not exist. A model based on invented inputs is worthless even with cautious assumptions.
2. An assumption can no longer be justified. If the assumed margin is above anything the company or its industry has ever achieved, the assumption merely expresses a wish.
3. The range is too wide for a decision. If the extreme scenarios are a factor of five apart, the result is unusable. “Cannot be valued” is a legitimate finding.
4. The business has changed fundamentally, for example through an acquisition worth more than 20% of the balance sheet total, a regulatory upheaval or the loss of a major customer. Under IFRS 8, customers accounting for 10% or more of revenue must be disclosed. In such cases, you recalculate from scratch instead of fine-tuning.

Every important assumption comes with a sentence that states when it counts as refuted. Examples are “If the EBIT margin falls below 13% for two consecutive quarters, the margin assumption is refuted” and “If days sales outstanding rise by more than ten days without a change in the business model, the question of whether the company can be valued is re-examined”. If such triggers are noted beforehand, you do not have to weigh up later whether a piece of bad news is bad enough. Without them, your judgement is guided mainly by your own purchase price.

The net pension obligation of €35 million comes from the IFRS financial statements. There it is calculated as the present value of the obligation minus plan assets, discounted under IAS 19 at the reporting-date yield on high-quality corporate bonds. In the HGB financial statements, the same obligation is shown at a different value, because Section 253(2) HGB discounts at the average market interest rate of the past ten financial years for the respective remaining term. Alternatively, the rate for an assumed remaining term of 15 years may be applied across the board. If the two sources are mixed, the bridge is wrong.

Since IFRS 16, the lease liabilities have been included in the €180 million of net financial debt. If you take them out, the lease expense has to go back into EBIT; otherwise the value rises purely as a result of the accounting.

Under IFRS, the goodwill of €195 million is only tested for impairment (IAS 36), whereas in the HGB financial statements it is amortised systematically, over ten years if its useful life cannot be reliably estimated (Section 253(3) HGB). A stress test is to calculate equity minus goodwill, that is, 340 minus 195 equals €145 million. This turns an equity ratio of 41% into 23%, based on a balance sheet total reduced by the goodwill. This does not change the DCF, but it does change the assessment of how much margin for error the company has.

The valuation delivers a range. The decision needs two further numbers that are not in the model: the required margin of safety and the position size. Both are set in advance, because they can no longer be chosen impartially afterwards.

mitnehmen: The walk-through starts with normalisation, not with the share price; €86.4 million of reported and €104.0 million of adjusted EBIT become a third figure of €92.9 million that you justify yourself.

The most influential assumption is rarely the one that gets the most attention; here, half a percentage point of WACC moves the value more than one and a half percentage points of revenue growth, because growth creates hardly any value when the ROIC is only slightly above the cost of capital.

If the multiple and the DCF contradict each other, the value whose assumptions are written down counts, even if the other is more convenient; a peer multiple contains the peers' assumptions without disclosing them.
The buying threshold and position size belong in the log before you look at the share price; otherwise the valuation merely serves to justify a decision that has already been made.
“Cannot be valued” is a legitimate result; a lack of cash flow coverage, changing auditors or a range spanning a factor of five end the calculation instead of refining it.

begriffe.text: Written list of every valuation assumption with its value, source, date, certainty assessment and the finding that would refute it. The log protects against adjusting the calculation after the fact until the result fits.

Operating profit adjusted for one-off and non-cash items, but not for recurring expenses that a company reports as special items. It typically lies between the income statement figure and the company's adjusted figure.
Sensitivity chart in which only one assumption is changed at a time and the resulting value is plotted against the base case. It shows which assumption the valuation depends on most.
Observable finding, set in advance, whose occurrence means that an assumption or the entire valuation counts as refuted, for example a margin below a threshold in two consecutive quarters.

Share of NOPAT that must stay in the business to finance the assumed growth. The relationship is g = ROIC × reinvestment rate. The rate prevents the terminal value from assuming growth without any capital requirement.
